lead: Numerical aperture (NA) is the one number that says how wide a cone of light a fiber accepts. It is built from the two refractive indices alone, so it is the first figure on any fiber data sheet and the starting point for coupling, mode count and cutoff calculations. The relative index difference Δ says the same thing as a fraction. Skew rays, which spiral round the axis without crossing it, are accepted over a wider cone than meridional rays, which matters when multimode fiber is launched from a broad source. Only a few universities teach the skew-ray part in detail; the NA formula is standard exam material.
prereq: You need: the acceptance angle from Ray theory: total internal reflection, acceptance angle.

sections.h3: Numerical aperture and the relative index difference

blocks.text: The acceptance derivation ended with n₀ sin θa = √(n₁² − n₂²). That quantity is defined as the numerical aperture:

blocks.where: NA is dimensionless; n₀ is the index outside the end face (air, 1); θ<sub>a</sub> is the acceptance half-angle; n₁ and n₂ are the core and cladding indices. In air θ<sub>a</sub> = sin⁻¹(NA).

blocks.text: NA does not depend on the outside medium: put the fiber in water and θ<sub>a</sub> shrinks, but n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> stays the same. Typical values are about 0.1 for single-mode fiber, about 0.2 for graded-index multimode fiber and 0.3 or more for step-index multimode and plastic fibers.
The relative index difference Δ expresses the index step as a fraction. Its exact definition and its usual approximation are:

blocks.where: The approximation uses n₁² − n₂² = (n₁ + n₂)(n₁ − n₂) ≈ 2n₁(n₁ − n₂), valid when n₁ and n₂ are close (weak guidance, Δ ≪ 1). Communication fibers have Δ of about 0.003 (single-mode) to 0.01–0.02 (multimode).

blocks.text: Rearranging the exact form gives n₁² − n₂² = 2n₁²Δ, so NA = n₁√(2Δ). With the exact Δ this is exact; with the approximate Δ it is very close.

A meridional ray lies in a plane that contains the fiber axis. Seen end-on it runs along a diameter, crossing the axis between reflections. The acceptance cone of the previous chapter is the result for these rays.

A skew ray enters off the axis and never crosses it. Seen end-on it traces a polygon of chords round the axis, and along the fiber it follows a helix. Two angles describe it: its angle θ to the axis, and the angle γ between its end-on projection and the radius at the point where it meets the wall. A meridional ray has γ = 0.

In a straight step-index fiber every reflection of a given skew ray happens at the same angle of incidence, so a skew ray that meets the TIR condition at one reflection meets it at all of them. For the same axial angle that incidence angle is larger than a meridional ray's, because the ray strikes the round wall obliquely. TIR is therefore met more easily, and the acceptance condition for skew rays becomes:

n₀ sin θas · cos γ = √(n₁² − n₂²) = NA
θas is the acceptance angle for a skew ray whose end-on projection makes angle γ with the radius. Since cos γ ≤ 1, θas ≥ θa: skew rays are accepted over a wider cone. γ = 0 gives back the meridional result.

Two practical effects follow. A broad source such as an LED launches many skew rays, so a multimode fiber collects a little more light than the meridional NA predicts, and a measured far-field NA can come out larger than √(n₁² − n₂²) over a short length. And skew rays travel longer helical paths, so they add to the spread of arrival times in multimode fiber (see Intermodal dispersion with signal degradation in fibers).

examples.question: A step-index fiber has n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.46 with air outside. Find (a) NA and the meridional acceptance angle; (b) Δ, exactly and by the approximation, and NA from n₁√(2Δ) with each; (c) the acceptance angle for a skew ray with γ = 45°.
steps: Check: 20.06° > 14.03°, as it must be, since cos γ < 1 widens the cone for skew rays.
examples.answer: NA = 0.2425 and θ<sub>a</sub> = 14.0°; Δ = 0.01342 exactly (0.01351 approximately, giving NA ≈ 0.2433); a skew ray with γ = 45° is accepted up to 20.1°.

traps: NA is a pure number. Writing NA = 14.0° mixes it up with θ<sub>a</sub>.
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²), not n₁ − n₂: for 1.48 and 1.46 the difference is 0.02 but NA is 0.2425.
State which Δ you use. (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ is the approximation; (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²) is exact and makes NA = n₁√(2Δ) exact.
Skew rays are accepted over a wider cone, not a narrower one: sin θ<sub>as</sub> = NA/cos γ is larger than NA.
A large NA does not make a fiber single-mode; it raises the V number and the mode count.

quiz.q: Define numerical aperture and write it in terms of the indices.
quiz.a: NA = n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub>, the sine of the acceptance half-angle times the outside index; for a step-index fiber NA = √(n₁² − n₂²).
It is n₀ times a sine; refractive indices are ratios of speeds and a sine is a ratio of lengths, so neither has a unit. Equivalently, √(n₁² − n₂²) is built only from pure numbers.

quiz.q: State one difference between a meridional ray and a skew ray.
quiz.a: A meridional ray lies in a plane through the axis and crosses it; a skew ray never crosses the axis and follows a helical path.

quiz.q: A fiber has n₁ = 1.50 and n₂ = 1.48 in air. Find NA, θ<sub>a</sub>, Δ (approximate) and n₁√(2Δ).
A multimode fiber has NA = 0.30. Find the acceptance angle for meridional rays and for skew rays with γ = 60°.
quiz.a: Meridional: θ<sub>a</sub> = sin⁻¹0.30 = 17.46°. Skew: sin θ<sub>as</sub> = 0.30/cos 60° = 0.30/0.5 = 0.60, so θ<sub>as</sub> = 36.87°.

quiz.q: A meridional ray and a skew ray have the same angle to the axis inside the core. Which is more likely to be guided, and why?
quiz.a: The skew ray. It meets the round wall obliquely, so its angle of incidence is larger than the meridional ray's for the same axial angle, and it can exceed θ<sub>c</sub> when the meridional ray's does not. Its incidence angle is the same at every reflection, so once trapped it stays trapped.

quiz.q: A data sheet gives NA = 0.20 for a fiber, but a short-length far-field test with an LED gives 0.22. Suggest a reason that is not a measuring error.
quiz.a: The broad LED launches skew rays, which are accepted and guided at angles beyond the meridional θ<sub>a</sub>; over a short length they have not yet leaked away, so the light leaves in a wider cone. Leaky rays near the edge of the cone add to this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Skew rays matter wherever a multimode fiber is launched from a broad source: fiber sensors, illumination bundles and the standard launch conditions used when multimode bandwidth is measured, where mode scramblers and mandrel wraps strip unwanted rays. Plastic optical fibers have NA near 0.5, so their skew-ray content is large. Search next for skew ray acceptance in step-index fiber, leaky rays and encircled-flux launch.
